```{r}
#Part A
#a.
students_scores <- c(Ana = 78, Ben = 92, Cid = 85, Dex = 92, Eli = 67, Fay = 88, Gio = 74)

scores <- c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74)
names(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio")

#b.
sort_ascending <- sort(students_scores)
sort_ascending

sort_decending <- sort(students_scores)
sort_decending

#c.
sort_ascending

#d.
subjects <- c("Science", "Math", "English", "Filipino", "History", "ICT")
incomplete <- c(85, NA, 90, 70, NA, 95)

#e.
sort(subjects)

#f.
sort(incomplete)

#Question 2
# Yes, because the vector was created with named elements, the names stayed correctly attached to their respective values during sorting.
#If it did not fallow their values, the data will be disorganized.

#Question 3
#Sort() silently removes Na, which is dangerous because it shrinks the dataset and drops missing data without warning.
```

```{r}
#Question 4
students_scores <- c(Ana = 78, Ben = 92, Cid = 85, Dex = 92, Eli = 67, Fay = 88, Gio = 74)

scores <- c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74)
names(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio")

sort_ascending <- sort(students_scores)
sort_ascending

sort_decending <- sort(students_scores)
sort_decending

subjects <- c("Science", "Math", "English", "Filipino", "History", "ICT")
incomplete <- c(85, NA, 90, 70, NA, 95)

sort(subjects)
sort(incomplete)

order(scores)
sort(scores)
#a. 
scores[order(scores)]
```

```{r}
#Question 5
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio")
score <- c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74)
section <- c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A")

students <- data.frame(name, score, section)
students

#a.
students[order(students$score), ]

#b. 
students[order(students$score, decreasing = TRUE), ]

#Question 6
#order(scores) returns a vector of integer positions(indices) that tell you where each element belong to achieve a sorted sequence.

#It only becomes useful and meaningful when you plug it into a square brackets to index and rearange a vector or data frame.

#Question 7
# sort() is built to operate on 1-dimensional vectors. If the attempt is to run a 2-dimensional data frame, R cannot process it because it doesn't know how to multiple columns simultaneously.

#order() generates a vector index position rather than changing the data itself.
```

```{r}
#Question 8
students_scores <- c(Ana = 78, Ben = 92, Cid = 85, Dex = 92, Eli = 67, Fay = 88, Gio = 74)
rank(students_scores)

cbind(scores = students_scores, rank = rank(students_scores))

#a.
cbind(scores = students_scores[c("Ben", "Dex")], rank = rank (students_scores)[c("Ben", "Dex")])

#b.
#Both of them recieved 6.5 cause R defaults to mid-ranks for ties.
```

```{r}
#Question 8
#a. 
sales <- data.frame(employee = c("Rey", "Sam", "Tin", "Uma", "Val"), units_sold = c(120, 145, 98, 130)
                    
sales$rank <- rank(-sales$units_sold)

sales

#b.
sales_ordered <- sales[order(sales$units_sold, decreasing = TRUE), ]

sales_ordered

#Question 9
#No, you cannot use order() alone to properly award ranks while also eordering the table.
#Order only shows you a sequence not the tied up and other value assigned.
```
